1About this document

Purpose

This document specifies the Portfolio Analytics Workspace: its layout, its functions and the analytics it presents. It describes what the system does and the result each capability produces. It is intended for portfolio managers and analysts reviewing the product, and for the product owner approving it. A separate handoff document carries the engineering detail.

Scope

The document covers the user interface: screens, controls, behaviour, and the figures displayed. It does not cover how the analytics service calculates its results, the source of its data, trading, order generation or investment recommendations.

Reference implementation

A working mockup accompanies this document and implements every function described here using fictional data. Its calculations demonstrate behaviour; they do not define production financial methods. Where this document and the mockup differ, this document governs.

Terms

Workspace
A saved working area containing the allocations under comparison, the analysis cards, the scenarios and the reporting currency.
Allocation
A named set of portfolio weights organised as a tree of categories and products.
Category
A named grouping of products and indices within an allocation. Its weight is the sum of the holdings in it. Categories belong to the workspace and are shared by every allocation in it; a workspace starts with the seven standard categories (Public Equity, Investment Grade Fixed Income, Other Fixed Income, Hedge Funds, Private Equity & Other Private Assets, Real Assets, Cash) and may rename, reorder, add and remove categories.
Product
An investable fund, ETF, index, security or uploaded return series held within a category.
Standard category
One of the seven categories of the platform taxonomy. Every instrument has a home standard category through its asset class, and each standard category has an index basket.
Snapshot
A read-only copy of an allocation fixed at a point in time.
Sleeve
A saved, versioned set of products with weights summing to 100%, reusable across allocations.
Reference
The benchmark or portfolio against which differences, active return and tracking error are measured.
Basis
Whether a figure is forward-looking (from capital market assumptions and the factor model) or historical (from realised or backtested returns).
Scenario
A set of overridden assumptions applied to selected allocations in place of the base case.
Card
A self-contained unit of analysis (table or chart) on the workspace canvas.
Factor model
A risk model (ISG or Axioma) that expresses holdings as factor exposures plus specific risk.

2Purpose and principles

The workspace supports the construction, analysis and comparison of multi-asset portfolio allocations in a single environment. It presents forward-looking and historical return, risk, contributions and factor exposures, and recalculates every figure when a weight, assumption or reference changes. Building a new allocation, modifying an existing one and comparing alternatives have equal priority and share the same screen.

The system's purpose is to make the consequences of an allocation decision visible before the decision is taken. Every change to an allocation is evaluated immediately against the same measures, the same assumptions and the same reference as every alternative under consideration, so that the difference between two allocations can be attributed to the allocations themselves and not to differences in how they were measured.

Structure

The system is organised in four layers. Each layer has a single responsibility, and each depends only on the layers beneath it.

LayerContentsResponsibility
Shared repositoriesSleeves, custom benchmarks, uploaded products, saved cards; the product library and index basketsHold the components that are defined once and reused across workspaces, each with its own version history
WorkspaceAllocations, the comparison set, the reporting currency, scenarios and the card arrangementHold one piece of analytical work in full, so that it can be closed, reopened, restored and shared as a unit
Analytical contextReporting currency, factor model, period, reference and active scenarioDefine the terms on which every figure is calculated, once, for all cards
AnalysisCards drawn from a catalogue of 36 entries, each with its own basis and settingsPresent the results for every allocation in the comparison set, in a consistent form

The workspace is the unit of work. It contains one or more allocations, of which any subset, up to six, forms the comparison set; one allocation at a time is the subject of construction. The comparison set may also contain snapshots, which are fixed and read-only, alongside live allocations, which change as they are edited. Every analysis card reads the same comparison set and the same context, and presents each member in the same order and colour, so that an allocation is identified consistently throughout the workspace.

Analytical results are produced by an analytics service behind a defined interface. The user interface submits allocations, context and scenario, and displays what the service returns; it performs no financial calculation of its own. Each card requests its own results, so a failure or delay in one card does not affect the others.

The allocation model

An allocation is a tree of three levels: the portfolio, its categories and the holdings within each category. A holding is a product or an index, and both are added in the same way. A category's weight is always the sum of its holdings: a change to a holding changes its category, and a change to a category rescales its holdings in proportion. No weight is held outside the holdings, so every figure the system reports traces to an explicit position. An allocation can be expressed in broad terms, with one index per category, in full product detail, or in any combination of the two, and its analytics remain complete at every stage of construction.

The categories are defined once per workspace, in a stated order, and every allocation in the workspace is analysed on the same category rows. A workspace starts with the seven standard categories of the platform taxonomy; categories can be renamed, reordered, added and removed to match the structure the portfolio manager uses. The taxonomy continues to classify instruments by asset class for the product directory, the sleeve repository, scenarios and benchmarks.

Weights may be negative or sum to more than 100% where leverage is permitted for the allocation. A sleeve, a saved and versioned subset of products within a category, can be applied to any allocation as a unit and remains linked to its source version. Allocations can be created empty, from a template, as a copy of another allocation, or from imported weights.

The analytical model

Every figure is calculated on one of two bases, and the basis is stated with the figure.

Forward-looking
Expected returns from the platform's capital market assumptions, adjusted by the active scenario where it applies; risk, correlations and exposures from the selected factor model. The basis answers the question of what an allocation is expected to deliver.
Historical
Returns realised over the selected period: the allocation's actual track record where complete position history exists, and otherwise a backtest of its current weights, with any product that lacks history before its inception represented by a stated proxy. The basis answers the question of how the allocation has behaved, or would have behaved.

The two bases are kept distinct throughout. A card is fixed to one basis, or presents both side by side; the two are never combined into a single figure. Measures fall into six families, each available on both bases where it is meaningful:

  • Return: total, excess over cash, and its passive and active parts relative to the reference.
  • Risk: volatility and its passive and active parts, tracking error, value at risk, expected shortfall, drawdown and diversification measures.
  • Efficiency: Sharpe and information ratios, and capture ratios against the reference.
  • Contribution: the share of return and risk attributable to each category, product, asset class or factor, presented so that the parts sum to the whole.
  • Exposure: sensitivity to each factor of the selected factor model, and the specific risk not explained by it.
  • Outcome: projected value ranges, probabilities of meeting a target, and the effect of historical and hypothetical stress events.

Two factor models are available, and the selected model governs every forward-looking risk figure and every factor-based measure in the workspace. Active measures are calculated against the reference set in the context, which may be a benchmark, another allocation in the comparison set, or each allocation's own assigned benchmark.

Core functions

Construction
Definition and modification of an allocation's categories, products and indices, with immediate validation of totals, leverage and coverage. Items requiring attention, such as unallocated weight, short histories or a missing benchmark, are collected and reported with the action that resolves each.
Optimisation
Mean-variance optimisation of the allocation under construction: minimum volatility for a target return, maximum return for a target volatility, or the trade-off between return and tracking error. The result is a proposal, presented with its efficient frontier and the changes it implies, and is applied only on explicit instruction.
Comparison
Side-by-side presentation of up to six allocations on common rows and a common context, with differences expressed either in absolute terms or relative to a chosen focus allocation.
Analysis
A free-form arrangement of cards selected from the catalogue. Every workspace begins with a summary of headline measures and a comparison of allocation weights; further analysis is added as required and can be saved as a reusable card.
Assumption testing
Scenarios that override expected returns, volatilities, correlations and factor premia for selected allocations. A scenario changes forward-looking figures only, is identified wherever it applies, and leaves the platform assumptions unchanged.
Reuse
Sleeves, custom benchmarks, products created from uploaded return series, and saved cards are held in shared repositories, versioned, and available to every workspace.
Persistence
Continuous saving of every change, with undo, a version history of the workspace, and restoration of earlier states without loss of fixed snapshots.

Design principles

  • One continuous workspace. Editing and analysis occur together. A weight change is reflected in every card without a separate calculation step, and the figures displayed always correspond to the current inputs or are marked as updating.
  • One stated context. Reporting currency, factor model, period, reference and scenario are set once and apply to every card that uses them. Two cards cannot silently answer different questions, and any card that departs from the shared context states the departure.
  • Like for like. Every allocation in a comparison is measured on the same basis, over the same period, against the same reference and in the same currency. Where data does not permit this, the adjustment made is stated.
  • Parts that reconcile. Contributions, attributions and decompositions sum to the total they explain, and are presented in a form that shows the sum.
  • Detail on request. The summary is presented first. Product rows, factor detail, method notes and data tables are available on demand and are not displayed by default.
  • Evidence, not advice. The system reports figures and differences. It does not rank allocations, recommend trades or apply changes without an explicit user action; optimisation results are proposals.
  • Visible data limitations. Backtests, proxies, incomplete coverage and unavailable values are labelled where they occur. An unavailable value is never displayed as zero, and the reason it is unavailable is stated.
  • Independent of the calculation source. The interface depends only on the analytics service's defined interface, so that the methods and data behind it can change without changes to the user interface.

3Layout

The workspace occupies a single screen. The allocation being edited is displayed on the left and the analysis on the right; the two areas share an adjustable split. All analysis updates in place when an input changes.

  1. 1
    Header. Workspace name, save status, undo and redo, Add allocation, export, and a menu for snapshots, versions, layout and reporting currency.
  2. 2
    Comparison strip. The allocations under comparison, each in a fixed colour used by every card. The allocation being edited carries an outline. Snapshots and sleeves carry a tag.
  3. 3
    Allocation rail. The allocation being edited, with four tabs: Build (category tree and weights), Optimize (mean-variance optimisation), Sleeves (reusable product sets) and Check (items requiring attention, with a count badge). The rail can be resized or collapsed to a strip of tab icons.
  4. 4
    Context bar. Reporting currency, factor model, period, reference (vs), projection horizon and band, the active scenario, and Add card. Each control appears only when a card in the workspace uses it.
  5. 5
    Card canvas. A twelve-column grid of analysis cards. Every workspace opens with two cards: Headline and, beneath it, Allocations side by side. Further cards are added from the card repository.

Secondary screens

Four libraries are presented as separate screens, each returning to the workspace unchanged: the workspace list, the sleeve repository, the benchmark library and the product directory. The card repository opens as a sheet over the canvas.

Workspace creation

A new workspace requires a name and a reporting currency. Every figure in the workspace is expressed in that currency: the Cash index, the risk-free rate, fixed-rate benchmarks, the FX factor and the currency stress test follow it. The currency can be changed later, with confirmation, and the change can be undone. Opening a workspace restores its allocations, cards, layout, scenarios and preferences as last saved.

4Allocation construction

An allocation is constructed in the rail's Build tab as a three-level tree: portfolio, category and holding. Categories are defined for the workspace as a whole, so every allocation in it is aligned on the same rows without mapping.

Weights

  • Holdings carry editable total-portfolio weights, with each holding's share of its category displayed alongside.
  • A category's weight is the sum of its holdings. Changing a holding's weight changes the category's weight by the same amount. Changing the category's weight rescales its holdings in proportion to their current weights (equally where they sum to zero). An empty category has a weight of zero, which becomes editable once it holds a product or index.
  • Weights are edited inline. Every committed edit recalculates all cards and is saved automatically.
  • Weights need not sum to 100%. The unallocated amount is displayed and earns no return and carries no risk; it is not treated as cash. Weights in other categories are never rescaled automatically.
  • Without leverage enabled, an edit that would raise the allocated total above 100% is rejected and the resulting total is stated.

Categories

Categories are created, renamed, reordered and removed in the tree, and each change applies to every allocation in the workspace. A new category takes any name not already in use, receives the next unused colour, is placed after the selected category, and appears at 0% in every other allocation. A category can be moved to any position in the tree, and the order is reflected in every card that groups by category. A category can be removed only when it is empty in every allocation. Each change is a single undoable step. This allows the tree to follow the portfolio manager's own structure, such as a thematic or liability-matching category, while comparisons remain aligned row for row.

A category on its own

Selecting a category in the tree turns it, for as long as it stays selected, into a temporary portfolio in its own right: the category's holdings rescaled to 100%, analysed by every card next to the compared allocations, and reweighted on every edit inside the category. It is measured against the same category of the reference, also rescaled. It is marked as temporary wherever it appears, is never saved, and ends when the selection moves to a product, when Esc is pressed in the rail, or when it is closed from the comparison strip.

Adding products

Each category row carries an add control (quick add) that inserts a search field beneath the category's holdings. For a standard category, results are limited to its asset classes, with a one-click extension to all categories; a category added by the user searches the whole product library. Results show identifier, type, history tags and any existing holding, and include indices as well as products. The / key opens quick add across all categories. A selected product or index is added to the category whose control opened the search, and its weight field receives focus.

Short and leveraged allocations

Short and leveraged positions are enabled per allocation. Once enabled, negative weights and totals above 100% are accepted, and gross exposure, net exposure and borrowing are displayed as information. The system applies no risk limits or approval gates.

Selection

Selection mode adds checkboxes to products. A selection bar reports the count and the categories spanned and offers sleeve creation. Selection never changes weights.

Check tab

The Check tab lists items requiring attention: unallocated weight, products without history, products proxied by a factor model, allocations without a benchmark, and a decision chain without a policy benchmark or an SAA. Each item links to its repair. The tab badge displays the count. Items for information only (no decision chain; products measured against their category index because they have no stated benchmark) are listed separately and are not counted.

Decision chain

An allocation can carry a decision chain: the portfolios its return and risk are decomposed through, from a policy benchmark (L0) through a strategic asset allocation (L1) and the benchmarks of its products (L2) to the allocation itself (L3). The steps between them are the SAA decision (S1), the product benchmark decision (S2) and the product or manager decision (S3). The chain is set from the rail header menu, beside Assign benchmark, and from the member menu in the comparison strip; the rail header notes when one is set. The dialog shows the four levels the chain resolves to and sets:

  • Policy benchmark: the assigned benchmark, or any version of a library benchmark, with the newer-version indicator.
  • SAA: an allocation in the workspace, a library benchmark, or derived from the allocation's category weights held in each category's index. An SAA can be created from the policy benchmark's constituents or from the allocation's category weights.
  • Product benchmarks: each product's stated benchmark, else its category index; the category index for every holding; or overrides per holding (a benchmark, an index or a product), reviewed in a mapping table.
  • Step order and implementation step: the order the three decisions are taken in, and whether the implementation step is one step or two (weights then benchmarks, or the reverse).

Saving the chain is one undoable edit. Snapshots, clones and drafts copy it. Levels are resolved from the chain on every calculation and never stored. A level that cannot be formed merges the steps either side of it; the other steps still compute. The SAA and product-benchmark levels can join the comparison as temporary members, following the rule for a category on its own: marked as levels, in a lighter tint of the parent's colour, analysed by every card, inheriting the parent's scenario scope, and never saved.

5Comparison and benchmarks

Comparison

A workspace compares up to six members. A member is a live allocation, a snapshot, a sleeve version or a benchmark. Every member appears in every card in its fixed colour. Removing a member from the comparison does not delete it. Selecting a member makes it the allocation being edited.

Reference

The vs control sets the reference used for differences, active return and tracking error. Three modes are available:

  • Shared benchmark: one preset or custom benchmark for every member.
  • Individual benchmarks: each allocation is measured against its own assigned benchmark. An allocation without one displays "No benchmark assigned" and no differences.
  • Compared portfolio: one member serves as the reference for the others.
  • Policy benchmark: each allocation is measured against the policy benchmark of its decision chain. An allocation without a chain displays "No decision chain" and no differences.

Benchmark library

The benchmark library holds preset benchmarks maintained by the platform team and custom benchmarks created by users. Presets are read-only and can be duplicated. A custom benchmark is built from indices, products, other benchmarks and at most one fixed rate (cash plus a stated margin), with a rebalancing rule and a visibility setting. Saving requires weights totalling 100%. Edits create a new version. An allocation retains the version it was assigned, and the picker indicates when a newer version exists.

6Optimisation

The rail's Optimize tab performs mean-variance optimisation of the allocation being edited. It uses the same assumptions, active scenario and factor model as the cards, so an applied result is consistent with every other figure in the workspace.

Objectives

  • Minimum volatility for a target expected return.
  • Maximum expected return for a target volatility.
  • Maximum expected return for a target tracking error to the allocation's benchmark.
  • Minimum tracking error to the allocation's benchmark for a target expected return.

For an allocation with a decision chain, tracking error can instead be measured to its policy benchmark or its SAA.

Targets default to the allocation's current values. The achievable range under the current constraints is displayed before the optimisation runs.

Constraints

  • Total weight is held constant.
  • Long-only weights, unless the allocation permits shorts.
  • A maximum weight per holding, 30% by default.
  • Optionally, each category within a band of its current weight, ±5 percentage points by default.
  • The assets are the allocation's holdings. A standard category's index basket joins only when requested, for held categories or for categories not held; its optimised weight becomes explicit holdings of its indices.

Results

The result presents the efficient frontier with the current and proposed allocations marked, expected return, volatility, Sharpe ratio, tracking error and information ratio before and after, and every weight change grouped by category. An unreachable target is reported together with the nearest achievable value. A result is marked out of date when the allocation, benchmark, scenario or factor model changes.

Application

The allocation is unchanged until the proposal is applied. Apply writes the proposed weights as a single undoable edit. Save as new allocation retains the original and adds the proposal to the comparison, so the two can be analysed side by side.

7Analytics cards

The analysis area is a free-form grid of cards drawn from a card repository: a catalogue of 36 entries plus cards that users have saved with their settings. The full catalogue is listed in Appendix A.

Opening cards

Every workspace opens with two cards: Headline and Allocations side by side. Allocations side by side presents the category weights of every compared allocation as stacked bars, in the workspace's category order. All other analysis is added from the repository as required, which keeps the initial view limited to the summary and the structure of each allocation.

Headline

The Headline card summarises every compared allocation on both bases. Measures are arranged as rows in four groups, and indented measures are components that sum to the measure above them. A Table / Focus switch at the top of the card selects one of two views; the selection, and the focus allocation, are stored with the card.

  • Table view (default). Each compared allocation has a forward-looking and a historical column, in comparison order, with the allocation being edited underlined.
  • Focus view. One allocation, selected from a row of buttons beside the switch and initially the allocation being edited, is presented first with its values in bold. Every other allocation is presented as its value minus the focus value, signed, on each basis. The view is the same as the Focus view of Drivers & Differences, so that differences are read the same way on both cards.
GroupMeasureDefinition
ReturnTotal returnExpected return (forward) or annualised realised return (historical)
Excess returnTotal return minus cash
· Passive excess returnThe benchmark's excess return
· Active excess returnTotal return minus the benchmark's return; passive and active sum to the excess return
RiskRiskVolatility: from the factor model (forward) or realised (historical)
· Passive riskCovariance with the benchmark divided by volatility
· Active riskCovariance with the active return divided by volatility; passive and active sum to the risk
Tracking errorVolatility of the active return; distinct from active risk
RatiosSharpe ratioExcess return divided by risk
Information ratioActive excess return divided by tracking error
99% value at risk1 day, 1 week, 1 month, 1 yearLoss exceeded with 1% probability over the horizon, as a percentage of value, from the mean and volatility of each basis

Forward-looking returns are taken from the platform assumptions, with the active scenario where it applies; every forward-looking risk measure is taken from the factor model. Historical measures are realised over the period. Passive and active measures use the reference set in the context bar; an allocation without a reference displays them as unavailable, with the reason stated.

Card structure

  • Subtitle: every subtitle begins with the card's basis (→ Forward-looking, or ◷ Historical followed by the period) and states the measure, unit and scope. A factor model or scenario is named only where the card departs from the context bar.
  • Body: the chart or table, with qualifying notes (coverage, proxies, basis per allocation) beneath it. The method appears under About these figures, closed by default.
  • Menu: rename, show data table, duplicate, save to repository, factor-model choice, remove. Every chart has an equivalent data table.
  • States: while updating, the previous result remains visible and is labelled. An unavailable result states the reason and offers a retry. A failure in one card does not affect the others.

Shared context and card settings

The context bar holds settings shared by all cards: reporting currency, factor model, period, reference, horizon and band, and scenario. Each card holds its own settings, such as basis, measure, units and view. Changing the period updates every historical card and no forward-looking card. Changing a card's setting updates that card only.

Attribution conventions are set once for the workspace, from the header menu: attribution model (Brinson–Fachler or Brinson–Hood–Beebower), interaction (in selection, in allocation, or its own effect), multi-period linking (Cariño, Menchero, GRAP, Frongello, or none), currency (in selection, or the FX factor row), unallocated weight (zero return, or cash) and fee basis (net of stated fees, or gross). A card that departs from them states the departure in its subtitle. A separate currency effect is listed but unavailable until local-currency returns are provided.

Layout

Cards are moved by dragging the header and resized from the corner, or with the arrow keys and Shift + arrow keys. A dropped card displaces the cards beneath it and the grid compacts upward. The layout is saved per workspace. Adding, removing, duplicating and changing a card's settings are undoable.

Chart conventions

  • Waterfalls for contributions. Every measure whose parts add up to a total opens as a horizontal waterfall, one allocation at a time, selected by tabs above the chart: return contribution, risk contribution (summing to the volatility, or to 100% as a share of risk), risk by factor, return attribution and the sources of active risk and return. Each step is labelled with its signed value; the total is drawn from zero beneath a rule. Bars or a table remain available in the card's settings.
  • Horizontal bars for exposures. Factor exposures are drawn as horizontal bars, one row per factor, with a bar per allocation.
  • Heat maps for change over time. Calendar-year returns, monthly returns and factor metrics over time are drawn as heat maps: blue for positive values, orange for negative, with depth proportional to size.
  • Emphasis. The legend controls which allocations are emphasised. Emphasis is shared across the cards of a workspace and never removes an allocation from a chart.

Saved cards

A configured card can be saved to the repository with a name. It stores the card type and settings but no data, and is available in every workspace with that workspace's context.

8Drivers & Differences

Drivers & Differences is the principal analysis table, added from the card repository. It presents what drives each allocation's return and risk, and how each allocation differs from its reference or from another allocation.

Measures

GroupMeasureRowsTotal
By productWeightCategories, expandable to products and index rows, then unallocated and totalAllocated weight
Return contributionExpected or realised return
Risk contribution (share of risk, or contribution to volatility)100%, or volatility
By factorExposure (β)One row per factor, sorted by size, with the largest eight shown and the remainder one click away—
Return contributionFactors, cash and specific sum to the return
Risk contributionFactors and specific sum to the volatility

A basis switch selects forward-looking or historical figures. Factor rows keep the table's width constant regardless of the number of factors in the model.

Views

  • Table. One column per allocation. Values are shown as contributions or exposures, or as differences from each allocation's reference. Factor cells include a bar diverging from zero in the allocation's colour.
  • Focus. One allocation is selected as the focus. Its values form the first column; each other allocation, and the focus's reference, is shown as its difference from the focus, with a diverging bar. This view isolates how alternatives depart from a single allocation.

Row selection

Selecting a category or product row makes it the workspace's selected row. Cards that follow the selected row (cumulative return, factor exposures, projections, scenario comparison, active risk & return) update their data and subtitle together. Expansion state is shared across allocations, and a row search filters the table while preserving parent rows.

Scenario columns

With a scenario active, each in-scope allocation displays a Scenario column and a Δ vs Base column. A Base | Scenario display is available as an alternative. Out-of-scope allocations retain a single column labelled with their assumption set.

9Factor models and active risk

Factor models

Two risk models are available. ISG has eleven factors: Equity, Term, Liquidity, Funding, FX, EM, Dollar, Size, Value, Commodities and Momentum. Axioma has the same eleven under the same identifiers, plus Credit, Short Volatility, Quality, Carry, Local Inflation and Local Equity. The FX factor is stated against the reporting currency. The platform's capital market assumptions remain the return model under both.

The context bar's factor-model switch applies to every card that uses a model. An individual card can be pinned to either model, and Compare with the other model adds a pinned copy beside it. A product not covered by a model takes its category index's loadings and is flagged. Under each model, factor contributions plus specific risk equal total risk. Factor-model risk does not change with a scenario, and cards state this.

Factor cards

  • Factor exposures: stand-alone exposures of the portfolio or the selected row, for every allocation, as horizontal bars; forward (model) or historical (estimated over the period).
  • Risk by factor: each factor's contribution to volatility, plus specific risk.
  • Factors over time: a heat map with factors as rows and calendar years as columns, showing exposure, risk contribution or return contribution for one allocation at a time. Each year's risk contributions sum to that year's realised volatility; return contributions, cash and specific sum to that year's return.

Active risk & return

The Active risk & return card separates each allocation's return and risk into a passive component (the benchmark) and an active component (the departure from it). It reports tracking error, information ratio and active share, and reconciles the parts in its notes: return equals passive plus active; risk squared equals passive squared plus tracking error squared plus the correlation term.

A single switch attributes both active risk and active return by factor, category, asset class or product:

  • By factor: active exposure multiplied by the factor premium implied from asset-class returns, plus specific.
  • By category or asset class: allocation and selection effects.
  • By product: each holding's active weight multiplied by its return relative to the benchmark.

Every attribution sums to the active return and the tracking error. The reference is the context bar's reference by default, or each subject's own benchmark, a selected portfolio, or a step of the decision chain, in which case the step's lower level is measured against its upper level. Its risk sources can be shown as tracking error or as parts of a parametric 99% one-year value at risk or expected shortfall. Return attribution, Rolling active return and tracking error, Factors over time, Active weights vs reference and Factor exposures accept a chain step in the same way; Drivers & Differences can show differences from the previous chain level, and Headline can split passive and active against each allocation's policy benchmark.

Decision chain card

The Decision chain card decomposes one allocation at a time along its chain, on both bases side by side or one, in six views:

  • Bridge: a waterfall from the policy benchmark's return to the allocation's, one bar per step; beneath it, the tracking error of the whole chain built from each step's contribution, or from stand-alone step tracking errors closed by the cross term, in tracking error, its share, or 99% value at risk or expected shortfall. Selecting a step opens it.
  • Levels: the headline measures of each level against the level before it, as a table or with one level in focus.
  • Steps: one step attributed by category, asset class, product or factor, with allocation, selection and interaction effects, or active exposure times factor return plus cash and specific; its risk by the same grouping. By product, the benchmark step compares each holding's benchmark with the SAA in its category, and the selection step compares each product with its benchmark.
  • Lens: the same step in asset and factor space side by side with a tie line, or as a matrix of groups by factors whose rows and columns tie to both.
  • Reconcile: each identity with both sides and the difference: the chain sums to the whole, each step ties across lenses, and the step tracking errors combine into the whole.
  • Over time: each step's linked contribution by calendar year or month, or rolling 36-month lines.

Its settings add the step order (including order-averaged, with the spread over every order), the implementation step, arithmetic or geometric active return, factor returns, holdings- or returns-based exposures, specific by group, ex-ante or ex-post risk, value-at-risk method (parametric, historical, or Monte Carlo), step risk, marginal and x · σ · ρ columns, and the other factor model side by side. Every view comes from one calculation, so the lenses tie exactly; returns-based exposures are the one setting that cannot, and the difference is shown with its reason.

10Historical data and coverage

Actual history and backtests

Historical figures use an allocation's actual history where complete position history exists, and otherwise a backtest of current weights rebalanced quarterly. Each column states its basis wherever the bases differ. When an allocation with actual history is edited, its historical figures switch to a backtest of the edited weights and the column is labelled Edited. The actual track record remains visible as a dashed series in the cumulative return card. Undoing the edit restores the actual basis.

Period

The period applies to every historical card. It defaults to the common history of the compared allocations, with presets for the last 1, 3, 5 and 10 years and custom months. A change in the available period caused by adding an allocation is stated.

Coverage

Products without return history are excluded from historical figures, and each affected card discloses the exclusion. Products whose history begins after the period start use their asset-class index before inception and are labelled as proxied. True zero, no exposure, partial coverage and unavailable values are displayed as distinct states.

11Scenarios

A scenario overrides the platform's assumptions for selected allocations without altering the platform model. Scenarios are stored with the workspace and affect forward-looking figures only; historical cards are unaffected and state this.

Assumption editing

  • The scenario drawer docks beside the cards so results remain visible during editing.
  • Expected returns, volatilities and correlations are editable at asset-class and holding level, and factor premia at factor level. Precedence runs from holding to asset class to factor.
  • Correlations are edited in a full matrix or in a pair editor. The two are synchronised and symmetric cells update together.
  • Overridden cells are marked. Each cell, group or the whole scenario can be reset.
  • A correlation matrix that is not positive semi-definite makes scenario results unavailable and names the scenario. Base results are unaffected.

Scope and display

A scenario applies to all compared allocations by default, or to a selected subset. Allocations outside the scope remain on the base case. The active scenario is named in the context bar and in every forward-looking subtitle. The Scenario comparison card presents the selected row under the base case and every workspace scenario.

12Sleeves

A sleeve is a named set of products with weights summing to 100%, filed under one category and stored in a repository shared by all workspaces. Sleeves allow a tested implementation to be reused without re-entering weights. Each edit creates a new version; earlier versions are never altered.

Creation

  • From a category: the category's products, rescaled pro rata to 100%. Weights of 5% and 3% become 62.5% and 37.5%.
  • From a selection: selected products, rescaled to 100% and filed under a chosen category. A selection spanning several categories is marked mixed.

Application

A sleeve applied to a category is added at a stated weight, either replacing the category's holdings or alongside them. A preview shows each product's weight before and after and the category's resulting weight. Applied products are tagged with the sleeve name and version, and the operation is a single undoable step. Applying copies the products; later edits to the sleeve do not affect the allocation.

Comparison

A sleeve version can be added to the comparison as its own column, fully invested at its own weights. Its analytics are then displayed in every card beside the portfolios. The column is fixed to its version and indicates when a newer version exists.

Repository

The sleeve repository lists sleeves by category, with search, versions, products and weights, and actions to add to a workspace, rename, re-file and archive. Archived sleeves are removed from search and application but retain their tags on allocations.

13Product directory

The product directory lists every product by category and displays the model's treatment of each. Products the platform does not hold can be added from a return history.

Product analytics

  • Forward-looking: expected return, volatility, Sharpe ratio and beta to the asset-class index.
  • Historical: annualised return, volatility, Sharpe ratio, maximum drawdown, best and worst months, correlation to the index, growth of 100 against the index, and calendar-year returns.
  • Factor: exposures under ISG or Axioma with specific risk.
  • Model treatment: a statement of how the model represents the product.

Products from returns

A cell range copied from Excel, with dates in the first column, one product per column and product names in the header row, can be pasted anywhere in the application or into the import dialog, or supplied as a CSV file. The parser recognises dates in common formats and Excel serial numbers. It accepts values as percentages, decimals or price levels, compounds daily and weekly data to monthly, and requires at least twelve months within the model's history. Gaps, partial months and suspected unit errors are reported per product.

Each product is fitted to the asset class whose index it tracks most closely, and filed in that class's category:

  • Expected return is cash plus beta times the class premium, with no alpha assumed.
  • Volatility is the product's own realised volatility.
  • Correlations are the class's, scaled by the product's correlation to the index.
  • Factor loadings are the class's, scaled by beta. Specific risk is the volatility not explained by factor risk.

Uploaded products appear in the directory and in quick add, tagged Uploaded. Once held, they are treated identically to platform products in every card. They can be renamed, their returns downloaded, and archived.

14Saving, versions and recovery

  • Continuous save. Allocations, cards, layout and scenarios save automatically. The header displays Saving, Saved or Not saved with a retry. A failed save retains the input.
  • Current results. Every result is tied to the input that produced it. A slower, older response never replaces a newer one, and the field being edited keeps focus while figures refresh.
  • Undo and redo. Construction edits, comparison changes, scenario edits and card changes are undoable. Card moves, resizes and display preferences are retained but are not undo steps.
  • Snapshots. A snapshot fixes an allocation's weights, categories and sleeve tags at a point in time, and copies its decision chain, which, like its benchmark, can still be changed. It is read-only and can seed a new draft. Editing a live allocation never alters its snapshots.
  • Versions and activity. A history records edits, sleeves created or applied, snapshots and scenarios, and allows earlier states to be restored as a new current state.

15Usability standards

  • Screen sizes. The primary target is a large desktop display. Below 1100 pixels the rail collapses and opens as an overlay. Below 900 pixels cards stack in a single column and the context bar wraps.
  • Keyboard. Every control is keyboard-operable, including weight editing, row expansion, card movement and resizing, and the scenario drawer. Shortcuts: / quick add, b collapse the rail, s scenario drawer, a add card, ? shortcut list.
  • Colour independence. Allocation and category colours are fixed palettes. Every chart carries text legends, headers and units, and a data table, so no figure depends on colour alone.
  • Change indication. Changed cells are highlighted briefly after recalculation without implying a favourable or unfavourable change. Reduced-motion preferences are honoured.
  • Visual economy. A setting is stated once, where it is set. Only exceptions carry tags (snapshot, sleeve, edited, proxy, coverage, no benchmark). Card tools and secondary controls appear on hover or focus.

16Release plan

The proposed sequence delivers a complete build, analyse, compare, test and reuse cycle first, and adds depth afterwards. The sequence is a recommendation for review and implies no schedule.

StageContent
P0 · Core workspaceTabbed rail with the category tree, workspace-wide category management, inline weights and quick add; allocation creation (blank, template, clone, import); live recalculation and continuous save; short and leveraged allocations; the context bar and card grid; Drivers & Differences; Allocations side by side and Cumulative return; the two opening cards (Headline and Allocations side by side); comparison of up to six members with basis labels and coverage states; the scenario drawer with scope and scenario columns; sleeve creation, comparison and application; keyboard operation and error recovery.
P1 · Depth and reuseThe remainder of the card catalogue, with waterfalls and heat maps; preset and custom benchmarks and the benchmark library; reporting currency; optimisation; active risk and return attribution; the product directory and products from returns; the ISG and Axioma factor models; saved cards and data tables; sleeve versions and archiving; extended scenario editing; snapshot workflows and version history.
P2 · RefinementExports with full context; extended layout preferences; additional shortcuts; extended import assistance.

Outside scope

Investment recommendations and optimiser-driven advice; trading, order execution and approval workflows; leverage risk limits; a cross-workspace scenario library; the platform's capital market model, index baskets and data services.

17Open questions

The following decisions remain open and require confirmation from portfolio managers and the product owner.

  • Optimisation and advice. The workspace reports evidence and does not recommend trades, yet the optimiser proposes weights. It remains to be confirmed whether proposals are acceptable as presented or require more neutral wording.
  • Residual treatment. Whether unallocated weight should ever be treated as cash.
  • Sleeve governance. Ownership, sharing and archiving rules, and whether a tagged category can be updated to a later sleeve version.
  • Metric conventions. Contribution conventions, annualisation, factor units, fee basis and historical factor coverage.
  • Snapshot reproducibility. Whether a snapshot also fixes assumptions, model version, market data, benchmarks and dates.
  • Multi-asset comparability. Currency hedging, valuation frequency, illiquid assets and proxies.
  • Benchmark inheritance. Which benchmark applies to a category or product, and how references with different holdings are aligned.
  • Workspace sharing. Private versus shared workspaces, and the handling of concurrent edits.
  • Analytics service. The source of the engine that evaluates arbitrary weights, targets and scenario overrides.
  • Decision chains. Whether a chain belongs to the allocation (as built) or the workspace; whether an SAA is edited as an allocation or governed as a benchmark; whether a snapshot fixes the resolved levels as well as the chain; whether derived levels should ever be saved; and whether forward-looking return attribution by step is wanted, or only risk.
